League of Nations. The first international organization designed to maintain peace and resolve disputes among member states, established in nineteen twenty after World War One as part of the Treaty of Versailles. It represented an idealistic attempt to prevent future wars through collective diplomacy and arbitration, though its effectiveness was severely undermined by the absence of major powers, notably the United States, the rise of aggressive regimes in the nineteen thirties, and its inability to enforce its own resolutions. It ceased to exist in nineteen forty-six, superseded by the United Nations.

The League was proposed by Woodrow Wilson as part of his Fourteen Points and formalized at the Paris Peace Conference in nineteen nineteen, embedded in the Treaty of Versailles. Ironically, the United States Senate refused to ratify membership, leaving it without its most powerful potential enforcer. Early membership excluded or limited the defeated powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria, as well as the Soviet Union, viewed as ideologically hostile. Crucially, the United States was also absent, making the League a club of European powers and their allies, not a truly universal body.

The League's Covenant established the principle of collective security: member states agreed to defend any member against aggression. It also created the Permanent Court of International Justice and the International Labour Organization. Yet the League failed at its most important tests. It condemned Japan's invasion of Manchuria in nineteen thirty-one but imposed no meaningful sanctions. Italy's invasion of Ethiopia in nineteen thirty-five was met with weak economic restrictions that did not deter. Germany's rearmament, remilitarization of the Rhineland, and annexation of Austria went unchallenged as the League had no military force.

The League's structure gave veto power to all member states in the Council, making enforcement of resolutions nearly impossible. Any single nation could block action, paralyzing the organization during crises. By the late nineteen thirties, the League was irrelevant to the major crises precipitating World War Two. Its final meeting occurred in nineteen thirty-nine, and it was formally dissolved in nineteen forty-six with its assets transferred to the newly created United Nations. The League's failure became the historical lesson for the design of the United Nations, which gave the five major powers permanent seats with veto power on the Security Council, a recognition that a peace organization needs the muscle of great powers. The League connects to World War Two, the war whose origins it failed to prevent or contain, to the United Nations, its successor organization designed with the League's failures in mind, to the Treaty of Versailles, the peace settlement that created it, to Woodrow Wilson, the American president who championed the League's creation, to the principle of collective security, which the League attempted to enforce but lacked means to implement, and to Italy, Japan, and Germany, the aggressive regimes the League could not restrain.
